name: Short Form (36) Health Survey
description: "The SF36 is a short questionnaire with 36 items which measure eight multi-item variables: physical functioning (10 items), social functioning (two items), role limitations due to physical problems (four items),role limitations due to emotional problems (three items), mental health (five items), energy and vitality(four items), pain (two items), and general perception of health (five items)."
plain-language_description: SF-36 is a set of generic, coherent, and easily administered quality-of-life measures. These measures rely upon patient self-reporting and have been widely used.

name: Stroke-Specific Quality of Life Scale
identified-from: Nobels-Janssen et al., Life Impact review
description: "The Stroke Specific Quality of Life Scale (SS-QoL) is a well known, standardised, disease specific measure to assess HRQoL after stroke that has been validated in patients with different types of stroke. The SS-QoL consists of 49 items in 12 domains and takes about 15 min to complete." The 12 domains are self-care, mobility, upper extremity, language, vision, work, thinking, family roles, social roles, personality, mood, and energy.
description_reference: Post, Marcel W. M., et al. “Development and Validation of a Short Version of the Stroke Specific Quality of Life Scale.” Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry [London], vol. 82, no. 3, March 2011, pp. 283–86, https://doi.org/10.1136/jnnp.2009.196394.
plain-language_description: The SS-QOL assesses health-related quality of life specific to stroke survivors.

name: Stroke-Specific Quality of Life Scale (Short Version)
description: The short version of the SS-QoL takes 1 question for each of the domains of the original instrument.
description_reference: Post, Marcel W. M., et al. “Development and Validation of a Short Version of the Stroke Specific Quality of Life Scale.” Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery and Psychiatry [London], vol. 82, no. 3, March 2011, pp. 283–86, https://doi.org/10.1136/jnnp.2009.196394.
plain-language_description: A 12-item version of the Stroke Specific Quality of Life scale developed to reduce the burden of the full version. It collapses the 12 domains from the full version into two dimensions - 'physical' and 'psychosocial'

name: EuroQol 5D  [3 level and 5 level versions]
identified-from: Andersen et al., Leung et al., Nobels-Janssen et al., Life Impact review
description: "The EQ-5D descriptive system is a preference-based HRQL measure with one question for each of the five dimensions that include mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression. The answers given to ED-5D permit to find 243 unique health states or can be converted into EQ- 5D index an utility scores anchored at 0 for death and 1 for perfect health. The EQ-5D questionnaire also includes a Visual Analog Scale (VAS), by which respondents can report their perceived health status with a grade ranging from 0 (the worst possible health status) to 100 (the best possible health status). Finally the specific utility (in clinical and research setting) of each one of them is discussed."
description_reference: “EuroQol-5D (EQ-5D): An Instrument for Measuring Quality of Life”. 2015. Monaldi Archives for Chest Disease 78 (3). https://doi.org/10.4081/monaldi.2012.121.
plain-language_description: There are multiple versions of this measure. It was first introduced as a 3-item questionnaire. Later, a 5-item version was developed to reduce the ceiling effects encountered on the 3-item version and increase the sensitivity of the instrument. In the 5 level version there are five dimensions: mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort and anxiety/depression. Each dimension itself has 5 levels: no problems, slight problems, moderate problems, severe problems and extreme problems. The respondent is asked to indicate his/her health state by ticking the box next to the most appropriate statement in each of the five dimensions. A second part of the instrument asks the respondent to rate their health from 0 - 100 by marking a cross on a line from "the best health you can imagine" to "the worst health you can imagine".

name: Health Utility Index
identified-from: Nobels-Janssen et al., Life Impact review
description: "HUI is a family of generic health profiles and preference-based systems for the purposes of measuring health status, reporting health-related quality of life, and producing utility scores...HUI evolved in response to the need for a standardized system to measure health status and HRQL to describe: 1) the experience of patients undergoing therapy; 2) long-term outcomes associated with disease or therapy; 3) the efficacy, effectiveness and efficiency of healthcare interventions; and 4) the health status of general populations."
description_reference: Horsman, John, et al. “The Health Utilities Index (HUI): Concepts, Measurement Properties and Applications.” Health and Quality of Life Outcomes [England], vol. 1, no. 1, October 2003, pp. 54–54, https://doi.org/10.1186/1477-7525-1-54.
plain-language_description: The Health Utility Index (HUI) is a standardized system for measuring health-related quality of life, providing utility scores that reflect individual health status for use in clinical studies and economic evaluations. The HUI is a family of preference-based instruments designed to measure health-related quality of life (HRQoL) across multiple dimensions. The HUI-2 measures seven health attributes — sensation (vision, hearing, speech), mobility, emotion, cognition, self-care, pain, and fertility. The HUI-3 measures eight attributes — vision, hearing, speech, ambulation, dexterity, emotion, cognition, and pain. HUI3 is generally considered more sensitive and has wider adoption in clinical studies and population health surveys.Each attribute is categorized into levels representing varying degrees of functioning or impairment. These levels are combined mathematically using preference weights derived from population-based studies to generate an overall utility score betweeo 0 and 1.

name: Quality of Life after Brain Injury overall scale
identified-from: Nobels-Janssen et al., Life Impact review
description:
"The Quality of Life after Brain Injury (QOLIBRI) assessment is a recently developed descriptive system for HRQoL after TBI. The QOLIBRI was
created in response to the need for a comprehensive disease-specific measure for TBI, and was constructed simultaneously in six languages by an international multidisciplinary team. The process of development was guided by WHO concept of QoL, and a model proposed by von Steinbüchelet al. The final version of the QOLIBRI is a 37 item scale with six subscales covering areas of wellbeing and functioning that are typically affected by TBI, and a total score which provides a summary of
HRQoL. The areas include the domains ‘cognition’and ‘self ’ that are not contained in generic health status measures such as the Short-Form-36 (SF-36)"
description_reference: von Steinbuechel N, Wilson L, Gibbons H, et alQOLIBRI Overall Scale: a brief index of health-related quality of life after traumatic brain injuryJournal of Neurology, Neurosurgery & Psychiatry 2012;83:1041-1047.
plain-language_description: The Quality of Life after Brain injury (QOLIBRI) is an instrument specifically developed to assess the health-related quality of life (HRQoL) of individuals after a traumatic brain injury (TBI). It includes the person’s perspective on the condition of their health, their overall functioning and wellbeing. The QOLIBRI has 37 items associated with four scales (Cognition, Self, Daily Life and Autonomy, and Social Relationships). Items in Part A measure satisfaction with various aspects of HRQoL while Part B measures issues that individuals feel bothered by after TBI e.g. Feelings and Physical Problems.

name: Sickness Impact Profile
description:
"The Sickness Impact Profile (SIP) is a behaviorally based self-report measure. It is an instrument that is used to gauge sickness-related dysfunction. It contains 136 items that are divided into 12 categories. In
addition to category scores and the overall score, the instrument can be used to calculate a physical and a psychosocial dimension score."
description_reference: de Bruin, A. F., et al. “Sickness Impact Profile: The State of the Art of a Generic Functional Status Measure.” Social Science & Medicine (1982) [Oxford], vol. 35, no. 8, October 1992, pp. 1003–14, https://doi.org/10.1016/0277-9536(92)90240-Q.
plain-language_description: The Sickness Impact Profile was developed to be broadly applicable across types and severities of illness, as well as across demographic and cultural subgroups. It was designed to evaluate various kinds of patient dysfunction in many different areas of activity. The SIP asks respondents to self-report the limitations of their activity. The respondent endorses statements that measure the activity that they actually perform that day, rather than what they believe they could perform. It can be adminsitered by an interviewer or self-reported. There are 136 questions across 12 categories. Scores are expressed as a percentage of dysfunction.

name: Visual Analogue Scale
description: "A Visual Analogue Scale (VAS) is a measurement instrument that tries to measure a characteristic or attitude that is believed to range across a continuum of values and cannot easily be directly measured.For example, the amount of pain that a patient feels ranges across a continuum from none to an extreme amount of pain. From the patient's perspective this spectrum appears continuous ± their pain does not take discrete jumps, as a categorization of none, mild, moderate and severe would suggest. It was to capture this idea of an underlying continuum that the VAS was devised. Operationally a VAS is usually a horizontal line, 100 mm in length, anchored by word descriptors at each end. The patient marks on the line the point that they feel represents their perception of their current state. The VAS score is determined by measuring in millimetres from the left hand end of the line to the point that the patient marks."
description_reference: Crichton, Nicola. "Visual analogue scale (VAS)." J Clin Nurs 10.5 (2001): 706-6.

name: Health Related Quality of Life 15D
description: "The 15D is a generic, comprehensive, 15-dimensional,standardized, self-administered measure of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) that can be used both as a profile and single index score measure... The present 15D questionnaire includes the follow-ing 15 dimensions: breathing, mental function, speech(communication), vision, mobility, usual activities, vitality, hearing, eating, elimination, sleeping, distress, discomfort and symptoms, sexual activity, and de-pression. Each dimension is divided into 5 levels, by which more or less of the attribute is distinguished."
description_reference: Sintonen, Harri. "The 15D instrument of health-related quality of life: properties and applications." Annals of medicine 33.5 (2001): 328-336.
plain-language_description: The 15D is a generic, self-administered instrument for measuring Health-related Quality of Life among adults (age 16+ years). It measures HRQoL across 15 dimensions including mobility, vision, hearing, sleeping, eating, speaking, going to the toilet,  mental well-being, and other aspects of daily life and health. Respondents choose one of five responses on each dimension. Scoring the 15D creates a single index measure (0 to 1).

name: Satisfaction with Life Scale
identified-from: Andersen et al., Life Impact review
description: "The Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS) was developed to assess satisfaction with the respondent's life as a whole. The scale does not assess satisfaction with life domains such as health or finances but allows Ss to integrate and weight these domains in whatever way they choose."
description_reference: Pavot, W., & Diener, E. (1993). Review of the Satisfaction With Life Scale. Psychological Assessment, 5(2), 164–172. https://doi.org/10.1037/1040-3590.5.2.164
plain-language_description: The Satisfaction with Life Scale (SWLS) is a brief, 5-item self-report tool designed to measure global cognitive judgments of life satisfaction. Using a scale from 1 to 7 respondents indicate their agreement with five statements about their life.

name: Patient Health Questionnaire
description: "The Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) is a self-report measure of depression consisting of nine items matching the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fourth Edition (DSM-IV) criteria of major depression. Respondents are asked to rate each of the items on a scale of 0 to 3 on the basis of how much a symptom has bothered them over the last 2 weeks (0=not at all, 1=several days, 2=more than half the days, 3=nearly every day). "
description_reference: Manea, Laura, et al. “A Diagnostic Meta-Analysis of the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) Algorithm Scoring Method as a Screen for Depression.” General Hospital Psychiatry [United States], vol. 37, no. 1, January 2015, pp. 67–75, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.genhosppsych.2014.09.009.
plain-language_description: The Patient Health Questionnaire 9 (PHQ-9) measures the frequency of depressed mood and anhedonia over the past two weeks.

name: 11-item version of Life Satisfaction Questionnaire
plain-language_description: The Life Satisfaction Questionnaire (LISAT-9, LISAT-11) contains 9 or 11 statements about different aspects of life and asks the respondent to rate their satisfaction with each.  It targets important life domains: life as a whole, vocational situation, financial situation, leisure situation, contacts with friends, sexual life, self-care management, family life, and partner relationships. The LISAT-11 has 2 extra items asking about the level of satisfaction of the individual’s physical health and psychological health respectively.

name: Aachen Life Quality Inventory
plain-language_description: The Aachen Life Quality Inventory is a pictorial adaptation of the Sickness Impact Profile (SIP) created to maximise aphasic patients' understanding of the verbal statements as well as to permit them to give nonverbal responses. Like the SIP the ALQI has 9 dimensions with 10 items each, but it adds two additional dimensions specific for aphasia and to explore neuropsychological complaints. The dimensions cover activity, movement, home management, social interaction, family relationship, ambulation, communication, leisure, self-support, plus cognition and language. A written version is also available.

name: Disability-adjusted life years
plain-language_description: "The disability-adjusted life year (DALY) is a societal measure of the disease or disability burden in populations. It is calculated by combining measures of life expectancy as well as the adjusted quality of life during a burdensome disease or disability for a population."

name: HSQuale
plain-language_description: HSQuale is a 54-item instrument specifically designed to measure the quality of life (QOL) of young patients with hemorrhagic strokes. It was developed based on the content of 40 open-ended patient interviews and has been validated for use in patients aged 18 to 49 years.

name: Patient-Reported Outcome Measurement Information System
plain-language_description: PROMIS® (Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System®) is a set of person-centered measures that evaluates and monitors physical, mental, and social health in adults and children. PROMIS measures are generic, rather than disease-specific, and can be used with the general population and with individuals living with chronic conditions.

name: Quality of Life in Neurological Disorders
description:
"Neuro-QoL is a set of self-report measures that assesses the health-related quality of life (HRQOL) of adults with neurological disorders. Neuro-QoL is comprised of item banks and scales that evaluate symptoms, concerns, and issues that are relevant across disorders (generic measures) along with instruments that assess areas most relevant for specific patient populations (targeted). The HRQOL domains included in Neuro-QoL were identified through several sources, including an extensive 
literature review, an on-line Request for Information (RFI), two phases of in-depth expert interviews (n=44 and n=89, respectively), patient and caregiver focus groups (N =11 groups) and individual interviews with patients and proxies (N = 63). On the basis of this input, 4 HRQOL domains and 17 sub-domains were chosen for adults.
plain-language_description: Neuro-QoL is a standardized tool to evaluate the physical, mental, and social impacts of neurological conditions like stroke, epilepsy, or multiple sclerosis. It evaluates health-related quality of life (HRQL) as a self-report questionnaire available in multiple formats (paper, computerised, short forms). Each domain uses self-reported questions, such as “How often did you feel tired?” for symptoms, “How much difficulty did you have with walking?” for function, and “I felt left out” for social impact. Moreover, questions employ a 5-point Likert scale (1 = least, 5 = most) based on frequency or difficulty.

name: Time trade-off
description:
"In health economics, time trade-off (TTO) is a technique used to measure the quality of life that a person or group is experiencing. An individual will be presented with a set of directions such as:

Imagine that you are told that you have 10 years left to live. In connection with this you are also told that you can choose to live these 10 years in your current health state or that you can choose to give up some life years to live for a shorter period in full health. Indicate with a cross on the line the number of years in full health that you think is of equal value to 10 years in your current health state.[1]

The answer given by the individual shows how many years in the current health state they would be willing to 'trade off', in order to regain full health. This answer can be used to calculate the individual's quality of life in that health state.

For example, an individual with severe asthma could be offered 10 years in their current condition, or a shorter length of time in full health. If this individual is willing to trade off two of the ten offered years in order to regain full health, this suggests that eight years in full health has the same value as ten years with severe asthma. In this case, the individual would have valued living with severe asthma at 0.8, relative to full health (defined as 1.0).

TTO scores can be influenced by socio-demographic characteristics and attitudinal variables of respondents, such as age, gender, marital status, having children, health status, education level, socio-economic status, ethnicity, and religious beliefs.[2] Also, they can be influenced by the effects of ill health on consumptive activities and non health-related utility.[3]

Time trade-off results are often used to calculate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), allowing healthcare decision makers to combine mortality and morbidity into a single interval scale."

name: Willingness to pay
description: "In health-related analyses, a willingness-to-pay threshold represents an estimate of what a consumer of health care might be prepared to pay for the health benefit – given other competing demands on that consumer’s resources."
description_reference: Bulletin of the World Health Organization
plain-language_description: "Willingness to pay determines how much a patient would pay for a hypothetical cure for all of their health problems"
